s=20
unclear to me because I ticked the box under "stratum" and "global" and t=

=20

Andrea.

messages.subject: Submersible transects and rock walls
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,
  I've been lurking for years on this list, but it's been some time since=
 I
have posted. I appreciate any help offered. Thanks in advance!

  I have some old submersible data (counts of Rockfish) that I would like=
 to
run through the distance program. I've done this with recent submersible
surveys successfully because we planned the survey properly so that we co=
uld
do line transect density estimation using distance. No problem there. The=

trouble is that I have several datasets from years ago that was not plann=
ed
correctly but would like to estimate density for.=20

  Unfortunately the submersible used in that survey had portholes on the
sides, not the front like the one we use now. The pilot simply followed
parallel to the rock wall so that it was to the side of the sub while the=

observers looked out and recorded their 'range' to the observed fish. Gue=
ss
what, everytime there was a rock wall almost all the distances are the sa=
me!
Why? Because rockfish cling to rock walls, the observers recorded them as=
,
for example, all being 2m from the sub. If the sub moved out 1m from the
wall, then they would all be recorded as 3m from the sub.=20

  I am guessing I'm out of luck with the line transect method, but does
anybody out there have any idea what I can do with these data to get a
density estimate?

Thanks again
Chris

--

Sumin George,

messages.subject: Estimating density for strata and CV
messages.subject_clean: Estimating density for strata and CV
messages.body_plain:
I am using DISTANCE to estimate density of different species of
songbirds in landscape blocks of 1 km2 with different levels of spruce
planting. There are four regions, each with 4 landscape blocks with
0-10, 10-20, 20- 30 and > 30% spruce. Within each block three habitat
types have been sampled: spruce, rich birch and poor birch. There were
three replicated point transects for each habitat type which were
samples three times during the breeding season. So the design is: 4
regions, 16 blocks, 144 points, 3 repeated measures in the season.=20

=20

I would like to calculate the density for habitat per block (eg. Spruce
in block1...block16, Rich block1...16, Poor block1...16), but the %Cv is
too variable ranging from 7.46 - 68.7% (772 detections of this
particular species). The whole point is, however, to calculate habitat
type per block. I am evaluating two alternatives:=20

=20

1.	restrict calculation to density for blocks using habitat type as
covariates. This gives me an estimate for blocks, but not for habitat
types. I don't find this a good option since there is a general interest
in the differences between spruce and the other habitat types. The
problem is that density is probably varying both in relation to degree
of fragmentation by spruce on landscape scale and habitat types. I
cannot pool density for habitat types across regions and landscapes
2.	The other option is to restrict my analysis to the distances
were detection prob =3D 1. I don't like this alternative either, because
it might not be enough data.=20

=20

Are there other things I could do to get a density estimate for habitat
types per block?

=20

--

messages.subject: heaping and cutpoints
messages.body_plain:
I have read in the Distance sampling book that cutpoints need to be at
least 5 in order to allow for the best model adjustments. I have some
heaping in my data, and the only cutpoints which give a proper histogram
is 33, 66, 100, which are three cutpoints. With proper I mean that the
first bar is larger then the next. It appears that there are some
evasive movements to about 30 m. Since I am also going to assess the
influence of covariates, I wonder if there are any problems of choosing
just 3 cutpoints. Will the comparison with covariates in the model be a
problem if there are only 3 cutpoints?

--

messages.subject: Question regarding Covariates and Pooling
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance Users,

I am working with a dataset where I have four treatments and four =
observers.  The treatments (burned, not burned, burned twice, burned and =
logged) have markedly different bird communities which presents an issue =
where each species tends to only be abundant in 1-2 treatments and I am =
faced with having to either pool/model as a covariate across treatments =
or observers in order to estimate density.  Here is the generalized =
question I would greatly appreciate feedback on:

Consider a 4x4 matrix for Observers A-D and treatments 1-4 for Species =
i. For each species, there are 4 observers and 4 treatments. Ideally, we =
would have enough data to estimate density in each cell (Obs x Trtmt). =
However, there is only enough data (e.g. >40 detections) such that one =
axis of the matrix (either Obs or Trtmt) needs to be a covariate or =
pooled across.=20
My guess is that the "usual" approach is that we would include Obs as a =
covariate or just pool across Obs since that is sampling issue (e.g. =
noise) and we want to estimate the treatment density. However, observer =
heterogeneity is high (detection probabilities differ within treatment =
--based on data from 3 species where adequate data exist to estimate Obs =
x Trtmt) and there are defensible reasons why you might expect the =
detection process to be largely similar across treatments with just =
differences in the scale of detection (e.g. same shape but just falling =
off at different distances). =20
Any feedback on the approach others have taken or thoughts on this would =
be greatly, greatly appreciated.  This strikes me as a common issue that =
must crop up frequently in DISTANCE analyses.

Thank you in advance,
Joe Fontaine

************************************
104 Nash Hall
Dept of Fisheries and Wildlife
Oregon State University
Corvallis, OR 97331

joe.fo...@oregonstate.edu

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi all
I am new to the list. I should start a bird monitoring survey in a belt =
of mountain ridge meadows. The objective study is to make seasonal =
comparisons in bird abundance and density: along the belt there are some =
grassland surfaces that were mowed for management (habitat improvements =
for priority conservation species) purposes..=20
The (only one) transect to be regularly visited is around 1,5 km long, =
and the survey will last one year cycle: I will use a GPS and a laser =
rangefinder.
Is one of the main assumptions (randomly placed lines) inherently =
disgarded or may I use coherently distance sampling, considering to =
partion the transect in a few subtransects or in temporal strata?
Thank you in advance
Luca Baghino Italy

messages.subject: Re: Enquiry
messages.body_plain:
Distance sampling is intended to allow inference beyond the sampled
plots.  If you have only a single line, you have no reliable basis for
doing this.  Your plot size is 1.5km long, and with a width determined
by the distance up to which you record birds, so plot size is determined
by your ability to detect birds.  It is difficult to envisage
circumstances where you would wish to choose plot size by that means.

Repeated visits do not generate independent data, so you cannot use
repeat visits as if these give you new lines.  Similarly, breaking your
line into segments does not allow you to say anything about densities
beyond your strip, because the segments are not independent samples from
a wider area.

Without knowing the objectives of your study, it is difficult to comment
further.

Steve Buckland
